study_identification.author_journal_year: Zhang et al., Journal of Affective Disorders, 2023
study_identification.title: Parsing the heterogeneity of brain-symptom associations in autism spectrum disorder via random forest with homogeneous canonical correlation

study_characteristics.study_objective: To identify ASD subtypes with distinct patterns of brain-symptom associations by using a normative model to estimate individual deviations from typical brain development, and then grouping cases according to their multivariate patterns of brain-symptom associations between individual deviations and core symptoms.

dataset_name.answer: Typically-developing participants of ABIDE I and II

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: CAT12 (Computational Anatomy Toolbox 12); SPM unified segmentation; AMAP segmentation; Geodesic Shooting registration; AAL3 atlas (140 brain regions excluding cerebellum and vermis)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Total intracranial volume (TIV) outliers removed (outside 1.5 IQR); 31 samples removed. Preprocessing failures excluded: 18 participants in ABIDE I and 14 participants in ABIDE II failed to complete segmentation. Overall, from preprocessing, 1094 participants in ABIDE I and 1100 participants in ABIDE II passed.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Normative modeling using multivariate linear regression (age, age^2, gender, TIV) was applied to reduce site effects. Residual data from normative model did not show significant site effects as demonstrated by t-SNE visualization showing no clear clusters by data collection site. BIC was used to select the best polynomial order of age (order 2 was optimal).

response_variable.answer: Gray matter volume (GMV) of 140 brain regions (AAL3 atlas, excluding cerebellum and vermis)

predictor_effects.answer: All predictors modeled as fixed effects in multivariate linear regression.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The paper addresses some nuisance structure by including age (with polynomial terms), gender, and TIV as covariates in the normative model. Site effects are evaluated post-hoc using t-SNE visualization showing no clear site clustering after normative modeling. However, the paper does not explicitly model site as a covariate or random effect in the normative model itself, relying instead on the assumption that residuals from the normative model inherently reduce site effects. Sensitivity analyses (eTable 2) show that correlations remain significant after regressing out age, age^2, gender, and TIV from canonical components, demonstrating robustness to these nuisance factors. The approach is indirect rather than explicit in handling site effects.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Site effect is generally an important problem for multi-center neuroimaging data analysis. Therefore, we have used the normative modeling to reduce its potential effect. Instead of the raw grey matter volume data, we used the residual data by referencing to the normative model. In this way, we reduced the variation across data collection sites... the residuals from the normative data have already reduced the impact of the site effects, as no clear clusters for the data collection sites can be observed. (eMethods 1); Since there were group differences in age, gender ratio, and TIV among the 4 subtypes, we regressed out these covariates from the CC-volume and the CC-symptom scores. In all subtypes, we found that the correlations remained significant between the residual component scores (eTable 2).
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Supplementary eMethods 1, page 2-3; Main text Sensitivity analysis section

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study employs a split-half validation approach within the same ASD case sample to assess the homogeneity index. For each identified CCA mode, the cases are randomly split into training (50%) and test (50%) samples. The weightings derived from the training sample are applied to the test sample, and the association between CC-volume and CC-symptom is tested for significance using 1000 permutations. This process is repeated 10 times, and the homogeneity index (Hs) is scored between 0 and 10 based on the number of times the association remains significant in the test sample. This is a clear example of validation using non-independent data within the same domain (the ASD cases from ABIDE).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Given a group of patients, we randomly split the group into two halves for training and test, respectively. For a CCA mode identified using the training sample, the weightings for both the canonical component of volumes (CC-volume) and the canonical component of symptoms (CC-symptom) were applied to the test sample. If the association between the CC-volume and CC-symptom remained significant (assessed by 1000 permutations) in the test sample, we added 1 to the index of homogeneity for the current CCA mode. The randomly split-half process was repeated for 10 times following the literature (Smith et al., 2015), and the final index of homogeneity was scored between 0 and 10.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study does not use an independent hold-out sample from ABIDE or another independent ASD dataset to validate the normative model. All validation is performed within the same ABIDE dataset using split-half cross-validation approaches. There is no mention of reserving a completely independent subset of ABIDE data or using external ASD datasets for validation.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: No text in the paper describes validation using an independent dataset within the same domain (e.g., a separate ABIDE cohort or independent ASD dataset).

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study does not validate the normative model using data from a different domain (e.g., different imaging modality, different population, or different clinical condition). All analyses are conducted within the ABIDE dataset using T1-weighted MRI data from ASD cases and typically developing controls. There is no mention of external validation using different datasets or domains.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: No text in the paper describes validation using data from a different domain.

clinical_dataset.answer: ASD participants of ABIDE I and II

deviation_metric.answer: Residuals from normative model (volumetric deviations); Canonical component scores (CC-volume and CC-symptom) from CCA; Homogeneity index (Hs) ranging 0-10 for assessing consistency of brain-symptom associations

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to identify multivariate associations between volumetric deviations of 140 brain regions and ADOS subscale scores. Random Forest with Homogeneous Canonical Correlation (RFHCC) algorithm to identify subtypes with homogeneous brain-symptom associations. Cross-loading analysis (Pearson correlation) to determine direction of associations (|cross-loading| > 0.1 and p < 0.05 uncorrected). Case-control classification using volumetric deviations and CC-volumes as features, with AUC as performance metric. Permutation testing (1000 permutations) to assess significance of subtyping improvement. Kruskal-Wallis H test for comparing clinical characteristics among subtypes. Chi-squared test for gender ratio differences.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Four ASD subtypes were identified with distinct brain-symptom association patterns involving frontoparietal regions (subtype 1), midbrain regions (subtype 2), ventral visual pathway (subtype 3), and social reward evaluation regions (subtype 4), with subtyping significantly improving case-control classification accuracy from 0.64 to 0.75.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Using the RFHCC algorithm, 4 ASD subtypes were identified, each with homogeneity index (Hs) = 10. All subtypes showed associations between volumetric deviations and the ADOS-social subscale score. Subtype 1 (n=47): positive association (r=0.859, p<0.001) with 39 brain regions showing positive correlations (r=0.29-0.44), particularly frontoparietal regions including right superior parietal gyrus, right inferior parietal gyrus, right medial orbital gyrus, and left inferior frontal gyrus. Subtype 2 (n=105): negative association (r=-0.648, p<0.001) with 14 regions, particularly midbrain regions including dorsal raphe nucleus, left ventral tegmental area, left pars compacta, left red nucleus (correlations ranging r=-0.20 to -0.31). Subtype 3 (n=110): negative association (r=-0.757, p<0.001) with 10 regions in the ventral visual pathway including left inferior occipital gyrus, inferior temporal gyrus, right middle temporal gyrus, and right fusiform gyrus (r=0.19-0.23). Subtype 4 (n=92): negative association (r=-0.697, p<0.001) with 6 regions including right anterior cingulate cortex and right pallidum (r=-0.21 to -0.25). The mean case-control classification AUC across 4 subtypes was 0.75 (range 0.64-0.91), significantly better than without subtyping (AUC=0.64, p<0.05 by permutation test) and better than k-means clustering approach (AUC=0.68, p<0.01). Subtypes showed significant differences in age, gender ratio, and TIV, but no differences in symptom severity scores or IQ. Associations remained significant after regressing out age, age^2, gender, and TIV covariates.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: First, the requirement for both neuroimaging and ADOS scores limited sample size due to missing data in ABIDE database. Future studies with larger samples are needed for validation. Second, midbrain nuclei (VTA, DRN) might be too small to be accurately mapped by automated alignment algorithms, so findings for subtype 2 need cautious interpretation.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The identified subtypes suggest that ASD heterogeneity might reflect changes in different subsystems of the social brain, including social attention (frontoparietal network in subtype 1), social motivation (midbrain regions in subtype 2), social perception (ventral visual pathway in subtype 3), and social evaluation/reward processing (ACC and pallidum in subtype 4). The RFHCC algorithm successfully identified homogeneous subgroups where conventional CCA on all cases failed (no CCA mode exceeded homogeneity index of 5 for all cases combined). Feature importance analysis showed that 100% (39/39) of brain regions associated with ADOS-social in subtype 1, 93% (13/14) in subtype 2, 40% (4/10) in subtype 3, and 17% (1/6) in subtype 4 contributed positively to case-control classification. This demonstrates that brain regions differentially associated with symptoms also drive diagnostic separation from controls.

general_notes.general_notes: This study proposes a novel RFHCC (Random Forest with Homogeneous Canonical Correlation) algorithm to identify ASD subtypes based on brain-symptom association patterns rather than neuroanatomical features alone. The algorithm uses singular value decomposition (SVD) for dimensionality reduction (first 5 principal components explaining >80% variance) as grouping features. Simulation experiments (100 repetitions) demonstrated the algorithm successfully recovered association patterns in all cases. The study compared RFHCC to traditional k-means clustering: k-means on volumetric deviations yielded 4 clusters but all had homogeneity indices <3, with mean classification AUC of 0.68; when applied to raw GMV (not residuals), neither RFHCC nor k-means could identify significant clusters, demonstrating the necessity of normative modeling. The canonical weights of CC-symptom showed that the social subscale had weight=1 while communication and stereotyped behaviors subscales had weight=0 across all 4 subtypes, likely due to high intercorrelation (p<1×10^-15). Correlation coefficients between canonical weight vectors of CC-volume across subtypes were all non-significant, confirming distinct patterns. The study emphasizes that 54% of brain regions showed inconsistent associations across subtypes (positive in one, negative in another), highlighting the importance of subtyping. Code is available at https://github.com/xdrzjj/ABIDE.
